experiences/pentecost-acts-2/title: Pentecost: wind, fire and tongues in Jerusalem
experiences/pentecost-acts-2/account: Acts 2:1-4 (KJV, public domain): "And when the day of Pentecost was fully come, they were all with one accord in one place. And suddenly there came a sound from heaven as of a rushing mighty wind, and it filled all the house where they were sitting. And there appeared unto them cloven tongues like as of fire, and it sat upon each of them. And they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance." Luke adds that pilgrims from many nations heard the disciples speaking in their own languages, that some mocked them as drunk, and that Peter explained the event as the fulfilment of Joel 2:28-32. About three thousand are said to have been baptised that day (Acts 2:41).
experiences/pentecost-acts-2/contemporar: Luke presents the event as the promised outpouring of the Spirit (Luke 24:49; Acts 1:8), the reversal of Babel and the birth of the Jerusalem church's mission. Peter's sermon reads it through Joel's prophecy of the 'last days'. Bystanders offered a naturalistic reading (drunkenness), which Peter rejects as it was only the third hour of the day.
experiences/pentecost-acts-2/assessments: Pentecost is the birthday of the Church and the inauguration of its sacramental life; the gift of the Spirit continues in baptism and chrismation/confirmation. Speaking in tongues is accepted as a real apostolic sign, though not regarded as the normative evidence of receiving the Spirit.

Acts 2 is a pattern, not only a one-off: a 'baptism in the Holy Spirit' distinct from conversion, often accompanied by tongues, is available to believers today. Classical Pentecostals (e.g. Assemblies of God) teach tongues as the 'initial physical evidence'.

Pentecost is a unique, unrepeatable redemptive-historical event marking the transition of the covenant; the tongues were real foreign languages that authenticated the apostolic message and ceased with the apostolic era.

Most critical scholars accept that the early Jesus movement experienced ecstatic phenomena (Paul's letters confirm glossolalia at Corinth), but see Luke's narrative, written perhaps 50 years later, as theologically shaped: the list of nations and the xenolalia motif serve his universal-mission theme.
experiences/pentecost-acts-2/debates/0: Were the 'tongues' known foreign languages (xenolalia), ecstatic speech (glossolalia), or a miracle of hearing?
experiences/pentecost-acts-2/debates/1: Is Spirit baptism subsequent to conversion (Pentecostal) or identical with it (most Reformed, Catholic and Orthodox readings)?
experiences/pentecost-acts-2/debates/2: Cessationism vs continuationism: is Acts 2 descriptive history or a normative pattern?
experiences/pentecost-acts-2/story:
The setting is Jerusalem a few weeks after the crucifixion of Jesus, around the year 30. Pentecost (Greek for "fiftieth") was the Jewish Feast of Weeks, Shavuot, celebrated fifty days after Passover as a harvest festival and, in some later Jewish tradition, as a commemoration of the giving of the Law at Sinai. It was one of the three pilgrimage feasts, so the city was crowded with Jews and proselytes from across the Diaspora. According to the Acts of the Apostles, the followers of Jesus, about a hundred and twenty people including the eleven apostles, Mary the mother of Jesus and his brothers, had been meeting in an upper room, praying and waiting, because the risen Jesus had told them to stay in the city until they were "endued with power from on high" (Luke 24:49; Acts 1:4-8). They had already chosen Matthias to replace Judas Iscariot (Acts 1:15-26).

Luke, the author of Acts, describes what happened on the morning of the feast. A sound "as of a rushing mighty wind" filled the house, something like divided tongues of fire rested on each of them, and they "began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance" (Acts 2:2-4, KJV). The noise drew a crowd. Luke lists the visitors by origin, from Parthians, Medes and Elamites in the east to Cretans, Arabians and visitors from Rome in the west, and reports that each heard the disciples speaking in his own language about "the wonderful works of God". Some were amazed; others mocked, saying the speakers were "full of new wine".

Peter, the fisherman from Galilee who only weeks earlier had denied knowing Jesus, then stood up with the eleven and addressed the crowd. According to Acts 2:14-36 he rejected the charge of drunkenness, since it was only the third hour of the day (about nine in the morning), and explained the event through the prophecy of Joel 2:28-32: in the last days God would pour out his Spirit on all flesh, so that sons and daughters would prophesy, young men see visions and old men dream dreams. He went on to proclaim that Jesus, whom the authorities had crucified, had been raised by God and exalted, and that it was he who had poured out what they now saw and heard.

Luke reports that the listeners were "pricked in their heart" and asked what they should do. Peter told them to repent and be baptised in the name of Jesus Christ for the remission of sins, promising that they would receive the gift of the Holy Spirit, a promise "unto you, and to your children, and to all that are afar off" (Acts 2:38-39). About three thousand people are said to have been baptised that day. The chapter closes with a portrait of the new community: devoted to the apostles' teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread and prayers, sharing goods, meeting daily in the Temple and in homes (Acts 2:42-47).

The only narrative source is Acts, written probably some decades later (most scholars date it between about 70 and 100, a minority earlier). Historians therefore read it carefully. Many accept a core memory of an early, collective experience of ecstatic speech and Spirit-possession among Jesus' followers in Jerusalem, since Paul independently attests tongues, prophecy and a sense of the Spirit's presence in his churches in the 50s (1 Corinthians 12-14). Others think Luke has shaped the scene theologically: the list of nations recalls the table of nations in Genesis 10 and reverses the confusion of languages at Babel, and the wind and fire echo Sinai. There is also a long debate about whether Luke means real foreign languages (xenolalia), an unintelligible speech heard as language (a 'miracle of hearing'), or something closer to the glossolalia Paul describes.

Whatever its exact form, the event became the founding story of the church's mission. Acts structures its whole narrative from it, as the gospel moves from Jerusalem to Judea, Samaria and "the uttermost part of the earth" (Acts 1:8). The feast of Pentecost was being kept by Christians by the second century, and by the fourth it was a major baptismal season. In East and West it is celebrated as the descent of the Holy Spirit and often called the birthday of the Church.

In the twentieth century the story took on new life. Charles Parham's students in Topeka (1901) and the Azusa Street mission in Los Angeles (1906) understood their own experiences of tongues as a restoration of Acts 2, and the movement they began took its name from it: Pentecostalism. For hundreds of millions of Christians today, this chapter is not only history but a pattern they expect to see repeated.
experiences/pentecost-acts-2/keyMoments/: Jesus' followers, about a hundred and twenty people, gather in Jerusalem to pray after his ascension, as Luke reports in Acts 1.
On the Feast of Weeks a sound like wind and tongues like fire come upon the gathered disciples, and they begin to speak in other tongues (Acts 2:1-4).
Pilgrims from across the Diaspora hear the disciples in their own languages; some are amazed and others mock them as drunk.
Peter preaches that the event fulfils Joel's prophecy and proclaims the crucified Jesus as risen Lord and Messiah.
About three thousand are said to be baptised, and a community of shared teaching, meals, prayer and goods forms (Acts 2:41-47).
Paul's letters from the 50s attest tongues and prophecy in his churches, independent evidence of early charismatic experience (1 Corinthians 12-14).
The Azusa Street revival in Los Angeles interprets its experiences as a renewed Pentecost, and the global Pentecostal movement takes its name from Acts 2.
experiences/pentecost-acts-2/significanc: Pentecost is the founding narrative of the Christian church's identity and mission: it gives the Holy Spirit a central place in Christian experience and frames the gospel as meant for every language and nation. Catholic and Orthodox traditions read it as the birth of the Church and connect it to baptism and chrismation or confirmation; Protestant traditions stress the preaching of the Word and conversion; Pentecostal and charismatic movements, now a quarter or more of world Christianity by some estimates, treat it as a repeatable pattern of Spirit baptism with tongues. Critical scholars debate how much of Luke's account is reportage and how much theological shaping, and what exactly 'other tongues' meant, but most accept that early Christianity was marked by intense collective experiences of the Spirit.
experiences/damascus-road-paul/title: Paul's encounter on the Damascus road
experiences/damascus-road-paul/account: Paraphrase of Acts 9:1-19 (also told in Acts 22 and 26): travelling to Damascus to arrest followers of Jesus, Saul is surrounded by a light from heaven, falls to the ground and hears a voice asking why he persecutes him; the voice identifies itself as Jesus. Saul is left blind for three days until Ananias lays hands on him, 'something like scales' fall from his eyes and he is baptised. In his own letters Paul says only that God 'revealed his Son' in him (Galatians 1:15-16) and that the risen Christ 'appeared' to him last of all (1 Corinthians 15:8).
experiences/damascus-road-paul/contempor: For Luke and Paul this was a resurrection appearance and a prophetic call to the Gentiles, not merely an inward change of mind. Paul treats it as the basis of his apostolic authority. In 2 Corinthians 12 he separately describes being 'caught up to the third heaven', which later mystics took as a model of rapture.
experiences/damascus-road-paul/assessmen: A genuine appearance of the risen Christ and the paradigm of conversion and vocation; the Feast of the Conversion of St Paul (25 January) has been kept in the West since the early Middle Ages.
A model for direct encounter with Christ, healing through the laying on of hands and being 'filled with the Holy Spirit' (Acts 9:17).

Paul's own testimony is first-hand and early (c. AD 50s), making this one of the best-attested religious experiences of antiquity; the three Acts versions differ in detail (who heard the voice, who saw the light), which scholars treat as Luke's literary variation.

Since William James the episode has been a classic case of sudden conversion; proposed explanations (guilt-driven crisis, temporal-lobe phenomena) are speculative and cannot be tested on a two-thousand-year-old report.
experiences/damascus-road-paul/debates/0: Was Paul's experience 'objective' (seen by companions) or visionary? The Acts accounts differ.
experiences/damascus-road-paul/debates/1: Is Paul's conversion a 'conversion' at all, or a prophetic call within Judaism (Krister Stendahl's question)?
experiences/damascus-road-paul/story:
Saul of Tarsus was a Greek-speaking Jew from Cilicia, a Roman citizen according to Acts, trained as a Pharisee and, by his own account, "exceedingly zealous" for the traditions of his ancestors (Galatians 1:14; Philippians 3:5-6). In the first years after Jesus' death the new movement of his followers was spreading among Jews in Jerusalem and beyond. Saul regarded it as a dangerous deviation. Acts places him at the stoning of Stephen, guarding the clothes of the executioners (Acts 7:58-8:1), and describes him going from house to house to drag believers to prison. Paul himself later admitted that he had "persecuted the church of God" and tried to destroy it (Galatians 1:13; 1 Corinthians 15:9).

According to Acts 9, Saul obtained letters from the high priest authorising him to arrest followers of "the Way" in the synagogues of Damascus and bring them bound to Jerusalem. The date is usually placed within a few years of the crucifixion, around 33-36. As he approached the city, a light from heaven suddenly flashed around him. He fell to the ground and heard a voice: "Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?" When he asked who was speaking, the answer came, "I am Jesus whom thou persecutest" (Acts 9:4-5, KJV). He was told to go into the city and wait for instructions.

His companions, according to Acts 9, heard the voice but saw no one; in the retelling of Acts 22 they saw the light but did not hear the voice. Saul got up blind and had to be led by the hand into Damascus, where he stayed three days without eating or drinking. Then a disciple in the city named Ananias, after objecting in a vision that this man was known for harming believers, was told that Saul was a "chosen vessel" to carry Jesus' name to Gentiles, kings and Israel. Ananias went to the house of Judas on the street called Straight, laid hands on him, and "there fell from his eyes as it had been scales". Saul was baptised and soon began preaching in the synagogues that Jesus was the Son of God, to the astonishment of those who knew why he had come.

Acts tells the story three times, once in narrative (chapter 9) and twice in Paul's own speeches, before a Jerusalem crowd (chapter 22) and before King Agrippa II (chapter 26), and the details vary slightly, which historians usually take as a sign of oral retelling rather than invention. Paul's own letters never narrate the scene, but they refer to it as an event in which the risen Christ "was seen of me also, as of one born out of due time" (1 Corinthians 15:8) and in which God "revealed his Son in me, that I might preach him among the heathen" (Galatians 1:15-16). He treated it as the basis of his apostleship.

The aftermath was complicated. Paul says that he went away into "Arabia" (probably the Nabataean kingdom) and returned to Damascus, and only after three years went up to Jerusalem to meet Cephas (Peter) for fifteen days (Galatians 1:17-18). Both Paul and Acts record a dramatic escape from Damascus, lowered in a basket through an opening in the city wall to evade arrest; Paul names the ethnarch of King Aretas as the one guarding the city (2 Corinthians 11:32-33; Acts 9:23-25). Believers in Jerusalem were at first afraid of him until Barnabas vouched for him (Acts 9:26-27).

From this turning point came the missionary career that carried the gospel through Syria, Asia Minor, Macedonia and Greece, and the letters that form nearly half of the New Testament books. Paul's insistence that Gentile converts need not be circumcised or keep the whole Mosaic Law, which he connected with the grace he himself had received, was debated at the meeting in Jerusalem around 49 and in his letter to the Galatians.

The phrase "Damascus road" passed into ordinary speech for any sudden, life-changing reversal. Historians and theologians have argued about what to call it. Traditional readings, especially since Augustine and Luther, see a conversion from guilt to grace. In 1963 Krister Stendahl argued that Paul experienced a prophetic call, like Jeremiah's, rather than a conversion from one religion to another, since he remained a Jew; later 'New Perspective' scholars developed related readings. Psychological and medical explanations, from visionary experience to epilepsy, have also been proposed, though the evidence for any diagnosis is thin.
experiences/damascus-road-paul/keyMoment: Saul, a zealous Pharisee, takes part in suppressing the Jesus movement, and Acts places him at the stoning of Stephen (Acts 7:58-8:3).
Carrying letters from the high priest, Saul travels toward Damascus to arrest followers of 'the Way' (Acts 9:1-2).
Near Damascus a light from heaven flashes around him and a voice identifies itself as Jesus whom he is persecuting (Acts 9:3-6).
Blinded, Saul is led into the city and fasts for three days before Ananias lays hands on him, his sight returns, and he is baptised (Acts 9:8-18).
Saul begins preaching Jesus in the synagogues of Damascus and then goes away into 'Arabia' (Galatians 1:17).
After escaping Damascus in a basket let down through the wall, Paul visits Peter in Jerusalem for fifteen days (2 Corinthians 11:32-33; Galatians 1:18).
Paul defends his law-free gospel for Gentiles at the meeting with the Jerusalem leaders (Galatians 2; Acts 15).
experiences/damascus-road-paul/significa: Paul's experience near Damascus made a persecutor into the most influential early missionary and author of Christianity, and his Gentile mission shaped the movement into a largely non-Jewish, transnational faith. His interpretation of the event as unearned grace became central to Western theology through Augustine and the Reformation, while the Eastern churches emphasise it as illumination and apostolic calling. Modern scholarship debates whether 'conversion' or 'call' best fits Paul's own understanding, a debate tied to larger arguments about Paul and Judaism. The story also became the archetype of the sudden conversion narrative that later evangelical and revival movements prized.
